To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the method is applicable to any model for GW emission and that the method can be used to exclude models for multiple events with a single network of GW detectors.

(i) the exclusion of a source model is a function of the network of GW detectors, the astrophysical population and its rate, the event rate distribution in the population, the event distance distribution, the GW emission model, the detector sensitivities and the detector noise, (ii) the exclusion confidence can be increased by combining the exclusion of multiple astrophysically distinct events, and (iii) the exclusion confidence is a function of both the GW emission model and the GW detector noise.

(1) a GW model can be observationally excluded if the GW emission is detectable in the network and the network has a sufficiently large sensitivity to the GW emission; (2) the GW model can also be excluded if the GW signal is not detectable in the GW detector network but the network has sufficient sensitivity to the GW signal, the event is sufficiently well localized, and the event rate is sufficiently high; (3) the GW emission can be excluded if the network has sufficient localization capability

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a framework to exclude theoretical models for astrophysical GW emission by using a null GW detection.
the method is a useful way to exclude a model for the emission of gravitational waves from a population of transient sources.

a null detection from the LIGO and Virgo network of GW detectors can rule out a theoretical model for the GW emission from core collapse supernovas at a confidence level of at least 90% (95%) for a rate of core collapse supernovæ of 1 per year (1 per 2 years) and for a network of 2 detectors (3 detectors).
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the context of a population of events, a null GW detection from a network can be used to exclude models for a subset of the population, provided that the population is sufficiently well characterized.
a null detection from an astrophysical source is not only a negative result but also a positive one, in that it can be used to constrain the source model.

, if the GW emission from a source model is sufficiently loud and the network of GW detectors is sufficiently sensitive, a null detection from the network will exclude the model with a very high confidence.
